```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)
library(viridis)
library(scales)
library(here)
library(knitr)

options(knitr.table.format = function() if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "pandoc")

source(here("R", "link_functions.R"))
source(here("R", "prior_sampling.R"))
source(here("R", "plotting.R"))

# Goal 1: Prior predictive results
summaries_pp  <- readRDS(here("output", "prior_predictive_summaries.rds"))
draws_long    <- readRDS(here("output", "prior_predictive_draws.rds"))

# RE prior predictive results
re_pp_summaries <- tryCatch(
  readRDS(here("output", "prior_predictive_re_summaries.rds")),
  error = function(e) NULL
)
re_pp_draws <- tryCatch(
  readRDS(here("output", "prior_predictive_re_draws.rds")),
  error = function(e) NULL
)
re_pp_available <- !is.null(re_pp_summaries) && !is.null(re_pp_draws)

# Goal 2: BF calibration results
summaries_bf  <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_summaries.rds"))
continuous_bf <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_continuous.rds"))

# Goal 2 extended: JZS comparison
jzs_available <- file.exists(here("output", "bf_calibration_jzs_summaries.rds"))
if (jzs_available) {
  jzs_summaries <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_jzs_summaries.rds"))
}
logbf_fig_available <- file.exists(here("figures", "logbf_distributions.png"))

# Goal 2 extended: Information / Lindley consistency simulation
consistency_available <- file.exists(here("output", "bf_calibration_consistency_summaries.rds"))
if (consistency_available) {
  consistency_summaries <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_consistency_summaries.rds"))
  cons_null200 <- consistency_summaries |>
    dplyr::filter(dist_b1 == "logistic", true_b1 == 0, n_subjects == 200)
  stopifnot(nrow(cons_null200) == 1)
  cons_q25_null200 <- cons_null200$q25_log10_BF10
  cons_q75_null200 <- cons_null200$q75_log10_BF10
}

```

## Full Simulation Design

### Implied Priors on the Probability Scale (Step 2)

The probability-scale analysis crossed the following factors:

- Link function: logit, probit (2 levels)
- Intercept prior family ($b_0$): Normal, Logistic, Cauchy (3 levels)
- Intercept prior scale ($s_{b_0}$): 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.50 (4 levels)
- Effect prior family ($b_1$): Normal, Logistic, Cauchy (3 levels)
- Effect prior scale ($s_{b_1}$): 0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00 (10 levels)

This yields $2 \times 3 \times 4 \times 3 \times 10 = 720$ conditions. For each condition, we drew 10 replications of 10,000 samples using the SimDesign package.

A separate probability-scale analysis for the random-effects hyperprior (referenced in the Random Effects Hyperprior section of the main text) held the fixed-effects priors at the recommended link-consistent configuration (Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept, Logistic(0, 0.25) effect) and crossed:

- Hyperprior family: Exponential, Gamma(shape = 2), Half-Normal, Half-Student-*t*(df = 3) (4 levels)
- Hyperprior mean: 0.15, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00, 2.50 (5 levels)
- Random-effects structure: random intercept only; random intercept + random slope (2 levels)

This yields $4 \times 5 \times 2 = 40$ conditions. For each condition, we drew 10 replications of 1,000 simulated studies with 50 subjects each, sampling the random-effects SD from the hyperprior and the fixed effects from their priors, and computed the implied subject-level success probabilities and condition effects.

### Bayes Factor Calibration (Step 3)

The BF calibration crossed:

- Intercept prior family: Logistic, Normal (2 levels; both at $s_{b_0} = 0.75$)
- Effect prior family: Normal, Logistic, Cauchy (3 levels)
- Effect prior scale: 0.25, 0.50 (2 levels)
- True effect ($b_1$): 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50 (5 levels)
- Number of subjects: 30, 60, 100 (3 levels)
- Trials per subject: 20, 50 (2 levels)

This yields $2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 5 \times 3 \times 2 = 360$ conditions with 100 replications each.

A separate random-effects simulation held fixed-effects priors at the recommended link-consistent configuration and varied only the hyperprior: Student-*t*(3, 0, 2.5), Gamma(2, 4), and Exponential(4), yielding 90 conditions with 100 replications each.

### Consistency Simulation

To verify the consistency behavior of Bayes factors under link-consistent priors empirically, we ran a focused simulation with the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) prior. We generated data under a between-subjects design: $N = 2 \times n_{\mathrm{subjects}}$ participants each contributing one binomial count from $n_{\mathrm{trials}}$ trials in a single condition ($x \in \{+1, -1\}$, sum-to-zero coded). We included participant-level random intercepts in both data generation and model fitting.

- Intercept prior family: Logistic (link-consistent; $s_{b_0} = 0.75$)
- Effect prior family: Logistic (link-consistent; $s_{b_1} = 0.25$)
- True effect ($b_1$): 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50 (6 levels)
- Number of subjects: 20, 30, 50, 100, 200 (5 levels; $n_{\mathrm{subjects}}$ denotes participants per condition)
- Trials per subject: 20 (fixed)

This yields $6 \times 5 = 30$ conditions with 50 replications each.

@fig-S-consistency shows the median $\log_{10}(\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ as a function of the true effect and the number of subjects. At each sample size, the median evidence grew with the true effect size. For true effects of 0.10 and larger, median evidence for $H_1$ grew with the number of subjects. For a true effect of 0.05, median evidence still favored $H_0$ up to 100 subjects per condition; such a small effect requires larger samples to be detected. Under the null, median evidence for $H_0$ grew from 20 to 100 subjects per condition. At 200 subjects per condition, the Bayes factors became very variable (under the null, the interquartile range of $\log_{10}(\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ spanned `r sprintf("%.1f", cons_q25_null200)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", cons_q75_null200)`). These Bayes factors were estimated with a kernel density estimate of the posterior at zero, which is imprecise for large Bayes factors, so we do not interpret the cells with 200 subjects. These results describe the simulated design and do not establish consistency in general.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S-consistency
#| fig-cap: "Empirical consistency behavior of the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25)
#|   effect prior. Points show the median
#|   $\\log_{10}(\\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ across 50 replications; ribbons (left panel)
#|   span the 25th--75th percentiles. Left: evidence as a function of true effect
#|   size, with one line per sample size (evidence grows monotonically with effect
#|   size at fixed $n$). Right: evidence as a function of sample size, with one
#|   line per true effect (sample-size consistency: evidence for $H_1$
#|   grows with $n$ for non-null effects; separately, under the true null the BF
#|   increasingly favors $H_0$ as $n$ grows). Dashed lines
#|   mark $\\mathrm{BF}_{10} = 3$, $1$, and $1/3$."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 10
#| eval: !expr consistency_available

library(patchwork)

cons <- consistency_summaries |>
  mutate(
    n_lab  = factor(n_subjects, levels = sort(unique(n_subjects))),
    b1_lab = factor(true_b1,    levels = sort(unique(true_b1)))
  )

hlines <- geom_hline(yintercept = c(log10(3), 0, log10(1/3)),
                     linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4)

p_info <- cons |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_b1, y = median_log10_BF10,
             colour = n_lab, fill = n_lab, group = n_lab)) +
  hlines +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25_log10_BF10, ymax = q75_log10_BF10),
              alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d("N subjects", option = "D", end = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d("N subjects", option = "D", end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = expression("True effect " * b[1]),
       y = expression(log[10](BF[10])),
       subtitle = "Evidence growth with effect size") +
  prior_theme()

p_lindley <- cons |>
  filter(true_b1 %in% c(0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n_subjects, y = median_log10_BF10,
             colour = b1_lab, group = b1_lab)) +
  hlines +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(cons$n_subjects))) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(expression(b[1]), option = "C", end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "N subjects (per condition)",
       y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Evidence growth with sample size") +
  prior_theme()

p_info + p_lindley
```

### JZS/Cauchy Comparison Simulation

To directly compare the link-consistent prior against the JZS/Cauchy default [@rouder2012], we crossed prior scale and design factors, fitting both effect-prior families to every simulated dataset:

- Effect prior scale ($s_{b_1}$): 0.25, $\sqrt{2}/2 \approx 0.707$ (2 levels)
- Effect prior family: Logistic, Cauchy (both fitted to each dataset)
- True effect ($b_1$): 0.00, 0.10, 0.20 (3 levels)
- Number of subjects: 20, 30, 50 (3 levels)
- Trials per subject: 20, 50 (2 levels)

This yields $2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 2 = 36$ conditions with 300 replications each; within every replication, both effect-prior families were fitted to the same dataset, so family comparisons are within-dataset.

### Density Formulas for Analytical Overlays

For the logit link with a $\mathrm{Logistic}(0, s)$ prior on $b_0$: $f(p) = f_{\mathrm{Logis}}(\mathrm{logit}(p), 0, s) / [p(1-p)]$. At $s = 1$, the logistic density and the Jacobian $p(1-p)$ cancel, giving $f(p) = 1$. For the probit link with a $\mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma)$ prior: $f(p) = \phi(\mathrm{probit}(p)/\sigma) / [\sigma \cdot \phi(\mathrm{probit}(p))]$, where $\phi$ denotes the standard normal density. At $\sigma = 1$, the normal densities cancel, again yielding $f(p) = 1$.


## Comparison to G-Priors for GLMs {#sec-gprior-comparison}

The main text describes two extensions of the g-prior to GLMs (see Related Work). Here we work out what they imply in the design of the running example: two conditions coded $x_i = \pm 1$, the logit link, and $N$ Bernoulli observations split equally between the conditions. Both priors were formulated for GLMs without random effects, so we consider the model without random effects. Throughout, the comparison prior is $\mathrm{Logistic}(0, 0.25)$, whose standard deviation is $0.25 \cdot \pi/\sqrt{3} =$ `r sprintf("%.2f", 0.25 * pi / sqrt(3))`.

*Generalized g-prior* [@bove2011]. The prior is $\beta \mid g \sim \mathrm{Normal}\big(0,\, g\,c\,(X'WX)^{-1}\big)$, with prior weights $W$ (here the identity) and $c = 4$ for the logit link [@bove2011, Eq. 6 and Table 1, pp. 389--390]. For the effect column, $X'X = N$, so $b_1 \mid g \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0,\, 4g/N)$. With a fixed $g$, the prior narrows as $N$ grows; the unit-information choice $g = N$ gives $\mathrm{Normal}(0, 2)$. With the Zellner--Siow hyperprior $g \sim \mathrm{Inverse\text{-}Gamma}(1/2, N/2)$, $g/N$ follows an $\mathrm{Inverse\text{-}Gamma}(1/2, 1/2)$ distribution for every $N$, and the marginal prior on $b_1$ is $\mathrm{Cauchy}(0, 2)$. We confirmed this numerically for $N = 40$, 400 and 4,000 ($10^6$ draws each). In this design, the generalized g-prior with the Zellner--Siow hyperprior therefore does not depend on the sample size. Its scale is eight times the scale of $\mathrm{Logistic}(0, 0.25)$. In other designs, the prior changes with $X'WX$, for example with unequal group sizes or more factor levels.

*Mixtures of g-priors with observed information* [@liclyde2018]. The prior is $\beta \mid g \sim \mathrm{Normal}\big(0,\, g\,J_n(\hat\beta)^{-1}\big)$, where $J_n(\hat\beta)$ is the observed information at the maximum-likelihood estimate. If both conditions have the observed success rate $\hat p$, the observed information for $b_1$ is $N \hat p (1 - \hat p)$, which we confirmed against the estimated variance of a logistic regression fit. For a given $g$, the prior standard deviation of $b_1$ is therefore proportional to $1/\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)}$: it is `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(0.25 / (0.9 * 0.1)))` times larger at $\hat p = 0.9$ than at $\hat p = 0.5$. The prior depends on the observed accuracy.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gprior-implied
#| tbl-cap: "Implied priors on the probability difference $\\delta p$ at three
#|   baseline probabilities $p_0$ (logit link, two conditions coded $\\pm 1$).
#|   Generalized g-prior: @bove2011 with the Zellner--Siow hyperprior, which
#|   reduces to $\\mathrm{Cauchy}(0, 2)$ in this design. Observed-information
#|   g-prior: @liclyde2018 with the unit-information choice $g = N$ and the observed
#|   success rate equal to $p_0$, which gives $\\mathrm{Normal}(0, 1/\\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)})$.
#|   Values are exact transforms of the prior on $b_1$."

gp_priors <- tibble::tribble(
  ~prior,                                    ~family,    ~scale_fun,
  "Link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25)",       "logistic", function(p0) 0.25,
  "Generalized g-prior, Zellner-Siow",       "cauchy",   function(p0) 2,
  "Observed-information g-prior, g = N",     "normal",   function(p0) 1 / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0))
)
gp_tab <- tidyr::expand_grid(i = seq_len(nrow(gp_priors)), p0 = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.9)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    Prior   = gp_priors$prior[i],
    s       = gp_priors$scale_fun[[i]](p0),
    q90     = q_abs_delta_p(0.9, eta0 = qlogis(p0), link = "logit",
                            family = gp_priors$family[i], scale = s),
    p_gt_03 = 1 - p_abs_delta_p(0.3, eta0 = qlogis(p0), link = "logit",
                                family = gp_priors$family[i], scale = s)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

gp_tab |>
  transmute(Prior, p0 = sprintf("%.1f", p0),
            s = sprintf("%.2f", s),
            q90 = sprintf("%.2f", q90),
            p_gt_03 = sprintf("%.2f", p_gt_03)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr", escape = FALSE,
               col.names = c("Prior", "$p_0$", "Scale of $b_1$ prior",
                             "90th percentile of $|\\delta p|$",
                             "$P(|\\delta p| > 0.30)$"))
```

@tbl-gprior-implied shows what these priors imply on the probability scale. Both g-priors place most of their mass on very large probability differences in this design. The link-consistent prior and the g-priors thus differ less in how they depend on the design than in their width: on the probability scale, the g-priors set a much stricter criterion for evidence in favor of an effect (see the criterion interpretation in Step 3 of the main text). In practice, g-priors are not readily available in `brms` or Stan, which limits their uptake in applied behavioral research.

### Properties Against Formal Criteria {#sec-bayarri-desiderata}

@bayarri2012 propose criteria for priors used in Bayesian model choice, grouped into basic, consistency, predictive matching, and invariance criteria. Here we assess link-consistent priors against the criteria that apply to them, compare them with g-priors, and state for each property whether it is established by a theorem in the cited source or only observed in our simulations.

*Information consistency.* For the Gaussian linear model with a fixed $g$, @liang2008 [pp. 412--413] show that the Bayes factor tends to a finite constant as $R^2 \to 1$ for fixed $n$ and number of predictors, which they call the information paradox. Mixtures of g-priors avoid it if the prior on $g$ satisfies the condition of their Theorem 2; the Zellner--Siow prior does, and the hyper-g prior does for $a \leq n - p + 1$ [@liang2008, pp. 415--416]. For link-consistent priors in binomial GLMs we have no such result. In our simulations, evidence grew with the effect size at a fixed sample size (see Consistency Simulation).

*Bartlett's paradox.* For fixed $n$, letting $g \to \infty$ makes the Bayes factor go to zero, that is, favor the null, regardless of the data [@liang2008, p. 412]. Link-consistent priors have a fixed, finite scale, so this limit does not arise.

*Model selection consistency.* As the sample size grows, the posterior probability of the true model should converge to 1 [@bayarri2012, Criterion 2]. For the Gaussian linear model, a fixed $g$ is not consistent when the null model is true; the prior on $g$ must depend on $n$ [@liang2008, p. 423]. The Zellner--Siow and hyper-g/$n$ priors are consistent for any true model, and the hyper-g prior is consistent except when the null model is true [@liang2008, pp. 416--417]. These results assume designs in which the models can be told apart asymptotically. For link-consistent priors in binomial GLMs we know of no general result. In our simulations, median evidence for the correct hypothesis grew with the sample size up to 100 participants (see Consistency Simulation).

*Invariance.* @bayarri2012 require that the units of measurement of the observations or the parameters do not affect the answers (measurement invariance, Criterion 6) and that answers be invariant under suitable transformation groups (group invariance, Criterion 7). Binomial outcomes have no units. The closest analogue for our design is invariance to the arbitrary labeling of the two conditions: under sum-to-zero $\pm 1$ coding and a prior symmetric around zero, reversing the labels reverses the sign of $b_1$ and leaves the Bayes factor unchanged. For g-priors, the corresponding properties depend on the design matrix.

*Predictive matching.* @bayarri2012 [Criterion 5] require that competing models have equal or close marginal predictive distributions for data of a minimal sample size, so that a minimal sample cannot discriminate between them. We did not examine this criterion. Our workflow uses a different and more modest property: the implied prior on the probability scale is known exactly (Step 2 of the main text), so the researcher can judge it directly. For g-priors in GLMs, the implied prior on the probability scale has to be computed for each design (see @tbl-gprior-implied).

*Computation.* @liclyde2018 obtain Bayes factors for mixtures of g-priors in GLMs from an integrated Laplace approximation with error of order $n^{-1}$ and implement them in the R package BAS. g-priors for GLMs are not available in `brms` or Stan.

| Property | Link-consistent prior | G-prior (fixed $g$) | Mixture of g-priors |
|-----------|:-------------|:-------------------|:--------------|
| Information consistency | Not established; evidence grew with effect size in our simulations | No (information paradox) | Yes, if the prior on $g$ satisfies Theorem 2 of @liang2008 (e.g., Zellner--Siow) |
| Avoids Bartlett's paradox | Yes (finite scale) | Yes for finite $g$ | Depends on the prior on $g$ |
| Model selection consistency | Not established; evidence grew with sample size up to 100 participants in our simulations | Only if $g$ grows with $n$; a fixed $g$ is inconsistent under the null | Zellner--Siow and hyper-g/$n$: yes; hyper-g: not under the null |
| Invariance to condition labels | Yes (sum-to-zero coding, symmetric prior) | Depends on the design | Depends on the design |
| Implied prior on the probability scale | Known exactly (Step 2) | Computed per design | Computed per design |
| Available in `brms`/Stan | Yes | No | No (BAS for GLMs) |

: Properties of link-consistent priors, fixed-$g$ priors and mixtures of g-priors, following the criteria of @bayarri2012. Results for g-priors are those of @liang2008 for the Gaussian linear model; @liclyde2018 study these criteria for g-priors in GLMs. {#tbl-bayarri-comparison}


## Full Bayes Factor Calibration Results {#sec-full-bf-results}

The main paper reports BF calibration results for a representative subset ($n_{\text{subjects}} = 30$, 20 trials, true $b_1 \in \{0, 0.10, 0.20\}$). Here we report the full results for the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) effect prior across all 5 true effect sizes, 3 sample sizes, and 2 trial counts.

### Detection Rates for the Link-Consistent Prior

@tbl-bf-detection shows detection rates ($P(\mathrm{BF}_{10} > 3)$) for the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) prior with a link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept prior. Under the null ($b_1 = 0$), the rate of misleading evidence for $H_1$ ($P(\mathrm{BF}_{10} > 3)$ under the null) stays below 5% in all conditions. Detection rates increase with effect size and sample size as expected, and are substantially higher with 50 versus 20 trials per subject.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bf-detection
#| tbl-cap: "Detection rates ($P(\\mathrm{BF}_{10} > 3)$) for the link-consistent
#|   Logistic(0, 0.25) effect prior across all simulation conditions. Columns
#|   show results for each combination of sample size ($n$) and trials per
#|   subject ($T$). Rows correspond to true effect sizes on the logit scale.
#|   Under the null ($b_1 = 0$), rates reflect misleading evidence for $H_1$.
#|   Each rate is estimated from 100 replications per condition; the Monte Carlo
#|   standard error of an estimated rate $p$ is $\\sqrt{p(1-p)/100} \\leq 0.05$."

rates_table <- summaries_bf |>
  filter(dist_b0 == "logistic", dist_b1 == "logistic", sd_b1 == 0.25) |>
  mutate(
    col_label = paste0("n=", n_subjects, " T=", n_trials)
  ) |>
  select(true_b1, col_label, P_BF10_gt3) |>
  mutate(P_BF10_gt3 = round(P_BF10_gt3, 2)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col_label, values_from = P_BF10_gt3)

knitr::kable(
  rates_table,
  col.names  = c("True $b_1$", colnames(rates_table)[-1]),
  align      = c("l", rep("r", ncol(rates_table) - 1)),
  escape     = FALSE
)
```

### BF Distributions Across All Conditions

@fig-S4-bf-full shows the full pattern of Bayes factor evidence across all conditions as a heatmap of median $\log_{10}(\mathrm{BF}_{10})$. Each cell shows the central tendency of the BF distribution for one simulation condition, with positive values indicating evidence for $H_1$ (an effect exists) and negative values indicating evidence for $H_0$ (no effect). The link-consistent prior yields calibrated evidence: under the null, median BFs are slightly below 1, reflecting appropriate support for $H_0$ with moderate-to-large samples.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S4-bf-full
#| fig-cap: "Median $\\log_{10}(\\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ across all simulation
#|   conditions for the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) effect prior with link-consistent
#|   Logistic(0, 0.75) intercept prior. Rows correspond to true effect sizes;
#|   columns to sample sizes. The two panels show results for 20 (left) and 50
#|   (right) trials per subject. Positive values (yellow) indicate evidence for
#|   $H_1$; negative values (dark) indicate evidence for $H_0$. Dashed contour
#|   at $\\log_{10}(\\mathrm{BF}) = \\pm \\log_{10}(3) \\approx \\pm 0.48$ marks the
#|   conventional BF = 3 threshold."
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 10

bf_heatmap_data <- continuous_bf |>
  filter(dist_b0 == "logistic", dist_b1 == "logistic", sd_b1 == 0.25) |>
  mutate(
    n_trials_label  = paste0("Trials per subject: ", n_trials),
    true_b1_label   = factor(paste0("b[1] == ", true_b1),
                             levels = paste0("b[1] == ",
                                             sort(unique(true_b1)))),
    n_subjects_fac  = factor(n_subjects)
  )

ggplot(bf_heatmap_data,
       aes(x = n_subjects_fac, y = true_b1_label, fill = median_log10_BF10)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", median_log10_BF10)),
            size = 3.2, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_trials_label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    name   = expression(median ~ log[10](BF[10])),
    low    = "#440154", mid = "grey90", high = "#FDE725",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits   = c(-1.5, 2.5),
    oob      = scales::squish
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete("Number of subjects") +
  scale_y_discrete("True effect size", labels = scales::label_parse()) +
  prior_theme() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```


## JZS/Cauchy Comparison: Full Results {#sec-jzs-full-results}

@tbl-S-jzs-rates gives full detection-rate results for the JZS/Cauchy comparison, supplementing the ROC and AUC analyses in the main paper. It shows $P(\mathrm{BF}_{10} > 3)$ (detection rate) and $P(\mathrm{BF}_{01} > 3)$ (false-null support) for both the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) and the JZS Cauchy(0, $\sqrt{2}/2$) prior.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-S-jzs-rates
#| tbl-cap: "Detection rates ($P(\\mathrm{BF}_{10} > 3)$) and false-null support
#|   rates ($P(\\mathrm{BF}_{01} > 3)$) for the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25) and
#|   JZS Cauchy(0, $\\sqrt{2}/2$) priors across all simulation conditions.
#|   Under the true null ($b_1 = 0$), $P(\\mathrm{BF}_{01} > 3)$ reflects correct
#|   support for $H_0$; under nonzero effects, it reflects false support for $H_0$.
#|   $n$: number of subjects; $T$: trials per subject. Each rate is estimated
#|   from 300 replications per condition; the Monte Carlo standard error of an
#|   estimated rate $p$ is $\\sqrt{p(1-p)/300} \\leq 0.03$."
#| eval: !expr jzs_available

jzs_tbl <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_jzs_rates_table.rds")) |>
  filter((prior == "logistic" & sd_b1 == 0.25) |
         (prior == "cauchy"   & sd_b1 > 0.7)) |>
  mutate(
    prior_label = if_else(prior == "logistic",
                          "Link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25)",
                          "JZS Cauchy(0, sqrt(2)/2)"),
    P_BF10_gt3 = round(P_BF10_gt3, 2),
    P_BF01_gt3 = round(P_BF01_gt3, 2),
    col_label  = paste0("n=", n_subjects, " T=", n_trials)
  ) |>
  select(prior_label, true_b1, col_label, P_BF10_gt3, P_BF01_gt3) |>
  pivot_longer(c(P_BF10_gt3, P_BF01_gt3),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "val") |>
  mutate(metric = recode(metric,
                         P_BF10_gt3 = "P(BF10>3)",
                         P_BF01_gt3 = "P(BF01>3)")) |>
  unite("prior_metric", prior_label, metric, sep = " | ") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = col_label, values_from = val) |>
  arrange(prior_metric, true_b1)

knitr::kable(
  jzs_tbl,
  col.names = c("Prior | Metric", "True $b_1$",
                colnames(jzs_tbl)[-(1:2)]),
  align  = c("l", "r", rep("r", ncol(jzs_tbl) - 2)),
  escape = FALSE
)
```

@fig-S-jzs-logbf shows the full distribution of $\log_{10}(\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ for all four prior combinations across the design space, underlying the ROC analysis in the main paper. At equal nominal scales, Logistic and Cauchy produce nearly identical distributions -- within each ridge, solid and dashed lines virtually coincide. The scale difference is the dominant factor: under the true null ($b_1 = 0$), scale 0.707 shifts the distribution substantially leftward relative to the $\pm\log_{10}(3)$ decision boundaries, reducing BF mass in the evidence-for-$H_1$ region. Prior scale moves BF mass relative to the decision thresholds; prior family does not.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S-jzs-logbf
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of $\\log_{10}(\\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ for all four prior
#|   combinations (Logistic/Cauchy $\\times$ scale 0.25/0.707) under the null
#|   ($b_1 = 0$), a small effect ($b_1 = 0.10$), and a medium effect ($b_1 = 0.20$).
#|   Rows show sample sizes ($N = 20, 30, 50$); columns show trial counts ($T = 20, 50$).
#|   Within each ridge, solid (Logistic) and dashed (Cauchy) lines nearly coincide
#|   at equal nominal scales. Scale 0.707 shifts both distributions leftward relative to
#|   the $\\pm\\log_{10}(3)$ decision thresholds (vertical dashed lines), reducing
#|   BF mass in the evidence-for-$H_1$ region."
#| out-width: "100%"
#| eval: !expr logbf_fig_available
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "logbf_distributions.png"))
```

@fig-S-jzs-heatmap shows the median $\log_{10}(\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ across all JZS comparison conditions as a heatmap, with the two priors in separate columns. This complements the distributional view by showing the full factorial pattern across sample sizes, trial counts, and effect sizes.

```{r}
#| label: fig-S-jzs-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Median $\\log_{10}(\\mathrm{BF}_{10})$ for the link-consistent Logistic(0, 0.25)
#|   (left columns) and JZS Cauchy(0, $\\sqrt{2}/2$) (right columns) priors across
#|   all simulation conditions. Rows: true effect size. Columns: sample size and
#|   prior. Panels: trials per subject. Positive values (yellow) indicate evidence
#|   for $H_1$; negative values (dark) indicate evidence for $H_0$."
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 11
#| eval: !expr jzs_available

jzs_continuous <- readRDS(here("output", "bf_calibration_jzs_continuous.rds")) |>
  filter((prior == "logistic" & sd_b1 == 0.25) |
         (prior == "cauchy"   & sd_b1 > 0.7)) |>
  mutate(
    prior_label    = case_when(
      prior == "logistic" ~ "Link-consistent\nLogistic(0, 0.25)",
      prior == "cauchy"   ~ "JZS\nCauchy(0, sqrt(2)/2)"
    ),
    n_trials_label = paste0("Trials per subject: ", n_trials),
    true_b1_label  = factor(paste0("b[1] == ", true_b1),
                            levels = paste0("b[1] == ", sort(unique(true_b1)))),
    n_subjects_fac = factor(n_subjects)
  )

ggplot(jzs_continuous,
       aes(x = interaction(n_subjects_fac, prior_label, sep = "\n"),
           y = true_b1_label,
           fill = median_log10_BF10)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", median_log10_BF10)),
            size = 2.8, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_trials_label, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    name     = expression(median ~ log[10](BF[10])),
    low      = "#440154", mid = "grey90", high = "#FDE725",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1.5, 2.5), oob = scales::squish
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete("n subjects / Prior") +
  scale_y_discrete("True effect size", labels = scales::label_parse()) +
  prior_theme() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))
```




## Supplementary Figures

```{r}
#| label: fig-S1-floor-ceiling
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of prior mass in the floor/ceiling region
#|   (p < 0.05 or p > 0.95) as a function of intercept prior scale and family.
#|   The link-consistent prior at $s_{b_0} = 1.0$ places exactly 10% in this region
#|   (2 x 0.05 = 0.10), confirming the uniform result. At $s_{b_0} = 0.75$,
#|   floor/ceiling mass drops below 10% for both link-consistent priors."
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 10

plot_floor_ceiling_heatmap(summaries_pp)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-S-floor-ceiling
#| tbl-cap: "Largest intercept prior scale $s_{b_0}$ for which the implied prior on
#|   the baseline probability places at most a given share of its mass outside
#|   the given bounds, for the link-consistent family of each link, and the mass
#|   outside the bounds at $s_{b_0} = 0.75$. Values are exact (computed from the
#|   prior CDF at the transformed bounds)."

readRDS(here("output", "t2_intercept_thresholds.rds")) |>
  filter((link == "logit" & family == "logistic") | (link == "probit" & family == "normal")) |>
  transmute(Link = link,
            Bounds = sprintf("%.3g / %.3g", lower, upper),
            threshold = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * threshold),
            max_scale = sprintf("%.2f", max_scale_exact),
            mass_075 = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mass_at_0.75)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = threshold, values_from = max_scale,
                     names_prefix = "Max. scale, ") |>
  relocate(mass_075, .after = last_col()) |>
  rename(`Mass outside at 0.75` = mass_075) |>
  arrange(Link, Bounds) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-S2-re-delta-p
#| fig-cap: "Effect size heterogeneity by hyperprior family and scale for the
#|   intercept + slope model. At equal mean, all families produce similar
#|   effect heterogeneity. Dotted lines mark +/-0.10, +/-0.20, +/-0.30."
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 12
#| eval: !expr re_pp_available

re_pp_draws |>
  filter(re_structure == "Intercept + slope") |>
  group_by(hp_family, hp_mean) |>
  slice_sample(n = 10000) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(hp_mean_label = paste0("mu == ", hp_mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = delta_p, y = hp_family,
             fill = hp_family, colour = hp_family)) +
  geom_density_ridges(stat = "binline", bins = 80,
                      alpha = 0.5, scale = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-0.30, -0.20, -0.10, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30),
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ hp_mean_label, ncol = 2,
             labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "D", end = 0.85, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expression(delta * italic(p)),
    limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = seq(-1, 1, 0.25)
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete("Family") +
  prior_theme()
```
